title: The blues: roots of all modern music
subject: art
description: Born in the cotton fields of Mississippi, blues invented the 12-measure grid and nourished jazz, rock, soul and hip-hop.

hero.hook: A cry in the cotton fields, and all modern music has a root.

blocks.text: Blues is not just a genre. It is the matrix of much Western popular music of the 20th century. It was born in the destitution of the cotton fields of **Mississippi**, at the end of the 19th century, as resistance and expression of African-Americans.
From jazz to rock'n'roll, from soul to hip-hop, its structures and emotion still irrigate our ears. Understanding the blues means going back to the source of a cry transformed into art.

Between **1870** and **1890**, in marked by segregation and the poverty of sharecroppers, the blues synthesizes African oral traditions. The [[Field hollers]] (solitary work cries) and the [[Work songs]] (songs timed to synchronize the effort) meet the [[Deep South]], religious songs sometimes carrying messages of freedom. [[Spirituals]]

The major innovation: the [[structure in 12 measures]], a grid of three chords which serves as a canvas for improvisation. The [[Blue notes]], inflected notes, imitate the pain of the voice. The guitar, often with a [[Bottleneck]] (glass or metal tube slipped over the strings), dialogues with the singer.
In the lyrics, the word “rider” often coded a lover, to address taboo themes in front of an uninformed audience.

sections.title: Robert Johnson and the Delta myth

blocks.text: The **Delta of MississippiEdit**, between Memphis and Vicksburg, is the cradle of **Delta blues**, a raw form of the genre. **Robert Johnson** (**1911**-**1938**) plays the wandering musician: only **29** recordings, an immense influence. His  treats the guitar like a miniature orchestra. [[Fingerpicking]]

blocks.caption: The Mississippi Delta: cradle of rural blues.
Robert Johnson: 29 titles, an eternal legend.

blocks.text: Legend has it that he sold his soul to the devil at a ([[Crossroads]]) in exchange for his mastery. The blues was then often called "the devil's music", compared to church songs. Johnson died of poisoning at a young age. *Cross Road Blues* and *Sweet Home Chicago* are becoming standards.
He recorded facing the wall in a San Antonio hotel room, not out of shyness, but to exploit the room's acoustics.

In the years **1940**, the Great Migration took millions of African-Americans to the industrial North. In **Chicago**, the blues becomes electrified to drown out the noise of the factories. **Muddy Waters** and **Howlin' Wolf** impose electric guitar, bass, drums.

blocks.caption: Muddy Waters in Chicago: blues connected to the current.

blocks.text: This electrification leads to rock'n'roll. **Chuck Berry** and **Bo Diddley** pick up the tempo. In the 1960s, the **Rolling Stones** (name taken from a Muddy Waters song) and **Led Zeppelin** re-exported these roots to white audiences, often without the original creators making a fortune.
Muddy Waters was "discovered" by musicologist Alan Lomax while he was still driving a tractor on a cotton plantation.

Jazz borrows structures and improvisation from it. Soul and R&B keep his voice visceral. Hip-hop recycles its heritage through the [[Sampling]] of old vinyl. **B.B. King** popularized the melodic guitar solo. More than a historical style, the blues remains a language about lost love, injustice and hope.
